response.title: what should i buy to power a food truck without a noisy generator
response.answer:
For a food truck, I'd recommend a commercial-grade lithium battery power system (LiFePO4) instead of a gasoline or diesel generator.

These systems are nearly silent, produce no exhaust, and can power refrigerators, freezers, lights, ventilation fans, POS systems, and even some cooking equipment.

The right system depends heavily on whether you're cooking with electricity or propane.

Three options worth considering

Solution

	

Best for

	

Approximate budget




Portable battery power station

	

Small food truck, refrigeration, lights, POS

	

$2,000–$6,000




Expandable battery system

	

Medium truck with several appliances

	

$5,000–$15,000




Custom commercial battery system

	

Full electric kitchen, heavy cooking loads

	

$15,000–$40,000+

These are rough system budgets, not verified current quotes.

Specific systems I'd look at
Shop

Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus Portable Power Station - EDM

3.84 kWh battery · 6,000W AC output

$2,999.99

Good for a small truck with propane cooking, refrigeration, lights, and other moderate loads. Expandable with additional batteries.

View product
Shop

EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra Inverter + 1 × Battery

6.14 kWh battery · 7,200W AC output

$4,199.00

Better for a larger truck or one needing 120V/240V power. Make sure you purchase the complete inverter-and-battery kit.

View product

For a permanently installed food truck system, I'd also investigate a 48V Victron inverter/charger with a 10–20 kWh LiFePO4 battery bank. This gives you more flexibility with shore power and electrical distribution, but requires professional design and installation.

How much battery do you need?

Food truck battery size calculator

Average power consumption

750 W

Operating hours per day

8 hours

Estimated battery capacity needed

7.5 kWh
Assumes approximately 80% of rated battery capacity reaches your appliances, accounting for losses and reserve. Actual requirements vary.

Remember that the inverter must also handle the maximum simultaneous wattage, including motor startup surges, not just average consumption.

What I'd actually buy

For a typical food truck with propane cooking, I'd aim for a 10–15 kWh LiFePO4 system, a 5–8 kW pure sine wave inverter/charger, and an overnight shore-power charging connection. Have a qualified mobile-kitchen electrician verify installation, electrical protection, weight limits, and local fire requirements.

Solar panels are optional. They can extend runtime but generally won't power a commercial kitchen by themselves. 
FTB
+1

Two questions that will determine the right purchase:

What appliances are you running? For example, refrigerators, freezer, exhaust hood, fryer, griddle, air conditioner, espresso machine. Are your cooking appliances propane or electric?

How many hours per day does the truck need to operate without plugging in?

With those answers, I can recommend an appropriately sized system, estimate its runtime, and narrow it down to specific products without overspending.
